clue.text: I'd exposure badly in tragedy

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters of the fodder are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone is lamenting that being badly exposed ended in tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophocles' play about the king who kills his father and marries his mother is the classic Greek tragedy.

clue.text: River rodent, the first to go extinct

indicators.note: the leading letter dies out, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a mouse is a small rodent

explanation.surface: A conservation story about a waterside rodent being the first species to die out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ouse is one of several English rivers of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ouse is a river in Yorkshire, and another flows through East Anglia.

clue.text: Farming authority regularly destroyed suede and fleece

parts.note: DEFRA is the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs

indicators.note: every other letter is wiped out, leaving the alternate ones

parts.note: its second and fourth letters survive

explanation.surface: A tale of a farming ministry ruining suede and sheepskin.
explanation.walkthrough: DEFRA is the British government department that oversees farming. 'fleece' looks like sheep's wool but is the verb meaning to cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to swindle them out of money, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Means of voting after Scotland raised tax

parts.note: post- is the Latin-derived prefix meaning after
Alba is the Gaelic name for Scotland

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something turns it to read bottom to top

parts.note: a toll is a charge or levy

explanation.surface: A political story about how people voted once Scotland put up its taxes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' applies only to the tax, so TOLL reads upward as LLOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Votes sent through the mail are a way of casting a ballot without visiting a polling station.

clue.text: Excellent drug lad's brought round

indicators.note: the boy's word is wrapped around the other piece

parts.note: a lad is a son; the 's is read as 'is'
pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: Praise for a boy who has delivered drugs, an unlikely commendation.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot-on is an informal British expression meaning exactly right or perfect.

clue.text: Preparation for viewers to look at ship

parts.note: to eye something is to look at it
a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: An invitation to spectators to come and admire a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'viewers' are eyes, and 'Preparation' is the cosmetic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: This cosmetic is applied around the eyes; viewers is a playful word for eyes.

clue.text: Mostly sound mistake

indicators.note: most of the phrase is kept, losing its last letter

parts.note: an alarm that goes off sounds

explanation.surface: Remarking that an error was largely a matter of sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' is the verb: an alarm sounds when it goes off. Run GO OFF together and drop the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A goof is an informal word for a silly blunder or error.

clue.text: Uneven quality of empty devotion in poems on saint

indicators.note: the emptied word sits inside the poems

parts.note: odes are lyric poems

indicators.note: the word is emptied of its middle, leaving its first and last letters

parts.note: only its outer letters are used

explanation.surface: A critic notes the patchiness of hollow piety in poems about a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty' keeps just the outside letters of 'devotion'; the poems wrap round them, and the saint follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddness here means the property of being odd, not even, like a number that will not divide by two.

clue.text: Digital growth if learning is distributed

indicators.note: the letters are spread around and reassembled in a different order

explanation.surface: A remark on how growth in the digital economy depends on spreading learning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' looks like computing, but it refers to digits, the fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: Nails grow at the tips of the fingers, which are digits; a playful definition.

clue.text: Persuasive son frequently gets work over in South Ken

parts.note: oft is an old word for often

indicators.note: the reversed piece goes inside the place name

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
Ken taken as written, as in South Kensington

indicators.note: turned over, so the word for work reads backwards

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A son often brings his work round to someone in South Kensington, a smart London district.
explanation.walkthrough: South Ken is the London district South Kensington; 'over' turns the opus abbreviation round before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking gently and quietly can be winning, so a mild-voiced manner is taken as persuasive.

clue.text: God sculptor's not got right

indicators.note: lacking something means it is taken out of the name

parts.note: Rodin was the French sculptor; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: Complaining that a sculptor has not got a god quite right.
explanation.definitionFit: Odin is the chief deity of Norse mythology.

clue.text: Book a specific couple of planes that take up gliders

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the second volume of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings

definitions.text: a specific couple of planes that take up gliders
definitions.meaning: second meaning: one particular pair of aircraft that tow gliders aloft

explanation.walkthrough: Gliders are hauled aloft by powered planes, which are therefore towers (things that tow); 'a specific couple' is the two.
explanation.definitionFit: The Two Towers is the title of the middle part of Tolkien's fantasy trilogy.

clue.text: Food is something eaten with biscuits by penguin

indicators.note: placed beside, so the two words sit together

parts.note: the macaroni is a crested penguin species
cheese and biscuits are served together

explanation.surface: A penguin is said to eat its food with biscuits.
explanation.walkthrough: The macaroni penguin is a real species; cheese and biscuits is a traditional British end to a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta baked in a cheese sauce is a familiar dish, the British name for mac and cheese.

clue.text: Conflict about action copy discarded daily?

indicators.note: the conflict word goes around the other pieces

parts.note: war is armed conflict
a step is an action taken
to ape is to copy

explanation.surface: A quarrel about a copied action and what gets binned each day.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as an example: a newspaper read and thrown away.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily newspaper that is thrown away becomes rubbish paper, an example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Disquiet from blood type being associated with fingerprints

indicators.note: joined up with, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: AB is one of the blood groups
dabs is British slang for fingerprints

explanation.surface: Forensic talk of a blood type linked to a set of fingerprints.
explanation.walkthrough: Dabs is police slang for fingerprints; the screaming abdabs is a British phrase for nervous terror.
explanation.definitionFit: The abdabs is informal British for a state of anxiety or nervous dread.

clue.text: Plane is cutting weight in offload

parts.note: a jet is an aircraft

indicators.note: something cutting into a word goes inside it

parts.note: a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: An aircraft trimming its load before it is dumped.
explanation.definitionFit: To jettison cargo is to throw it overboard to lighten a vessel, to dump it.

clue.text: Literary character, another I altered

indicators.note: changed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A writer altered yet another letter in the manuscript.
explanation.definitionFit: A protagonist lacking conventional heroic qualities is a type of character in fiction.

clue.text: Stomach jewellery rapidly losing value

parts.note: tum is a childish word for stomach
bling is flashy jewellery

explanation.surface: A belly-button ring whose price is crashing.
explanation.definitionFit: Prices that are falling sharply are said to be plummeting, as shares tumble.

clue.text: Islander with French mother outside New Cross

indicators.note: the French word sits outside the other pieces

parts.note: maman is French for mum
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: An islander whose French mother is standing outside New Cross, a district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: New Cross is a district of south-east London, a distraction here.
explanation.definitionFit: A Manxman comes from the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea.

clue.text: Jungle Book role's cut line in private

parts.note: to mow grass is to cut it

indicators.note: the line letter goes inside the soldier

parts.note: a GI is a US private soldier

explanation.surface: A part in a Jungle Book production is cut in a private rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is', linking definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's man-cub raised by wolves is the central figure of the stories.

clue.text: Travel diversion in Hampshire town

parts.note: to go is to travel
sport is amusement or pastime

explanation.surface: A road diversion while travelling in Hampshire, a county in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Gosport is a naval town on the south coast facing Portsmouth across the harbour.

clue.text: Parody finishes with the raising of spades

indicators.note: in a down entry, a letter raised moves higher, to the top

parts.note: to end up is to finish
S is the card-suit abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A card game ending when spades are played high.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ENDS UP (finishes) and lift the S from the middle to the top of this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A send-up is a mocking imitation, a British term for a satire or lampoon.

clue.text: Funnily metamorphose in …. this?

indicators.note: done in a comic way, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Asks what a comic transformation would produce.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: two actors comically transform into a stage animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Two performers in one costume become a comic pretend animal in a British Christmas pantomime show.

clue.text: Curdled milk runs under container for fantastic pie?

indicators.note: in a down entry the runs letter goes below

parts.note: pie in the sky is a fantasy, so the sky contains it
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Milk curdling in a dish under a pie.
explanation.walkthrough: Pie in the sky is an idiom for an unrealistic hope.
explanation.definitionFit: Skyr is an Icelandic cultured dairy product, thick like yoghurt.

clue.text: Report about mass ceremony

indicators.note: the bang goes around the other letter

parts.note: a pop is the report of a gun or cork
M is the physics symbol for mass

explanation.surface: A news report about a religious mass ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' is a bang, not a news item.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomp is splendid display, as in the phrase pomp and circumstance.

clue.text: What unemployed Parisian does embroidery?

parts.note: what a jobless person must do is need (a job)
le is the French for the, as a Parisian would say it
to work is to do, operate or function

explanation.surface: Asks what a jobless person in Paris does with their time.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the jobless Parisian 'needs le work', Franglais for needing the work; the split into three parts is a convenience.
explanation.definitionFit: Embroidery is decorative stitching done with a needle, a kind of sewing craft.

clue.text: Outfit introducing new phone

indicators.note: the outfit takes in another letter

parts.note: a rig is a set of clothes or equipment

explanation.surface: A clothing brand launches a new mobile.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring someone is British for calling them on the telephone.

clue.text: Worker in print company ordered import covering operating system

indicators.note: the rearranged word wraps round the other piece
put in order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: OS is the computing abbreviation

explanation.surface: A print firm ordered an imported operating system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges the letters of 'import' so that they wrap round the computing abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A compositor sets type for printing, a traditional trade in the press.
